I can think of a few:

-usenet/newsgroups: today it is little more than a bittorrent alternative. While it does have it's advantages over bittorrent (consistently high speeds, security) but costs a lot more than a decent VPN to gain access and depends on a handful of datacenters for survival. Usenet also has less content available and more spam than sites like kickasstorrents and thepiratebay.

-cable TV: if you don't watch sports, you really could replace it with the internet. And I predict sports will eventually go in the direction of online streams or pay per view.

-landline phones: being replaced by cell phones and much cheaper voip services

-Conventional HDDs: I remember the days when a 250 GB hard drive would cost as much as a 250 GB SSD today. If HDD prices ever go up again due to flooding in Thailand, etc new HDDs could stop being sold in a heartbeat. SSDs are also technically superior in most if not all aspects. HDDs have the second highest fail rate of all computer components (laptop power adapters being #1).

-paper: personally, I would love to live in a world where paper is illegal and I never have to deal with anything that can't be downloaded and viewed on a screen. When I have college professors who still insist on turning in and returning physical paper assignments, it creates 95% of the clutter in my room. It's also very easy for paper to get lost or damaged compared to a .docx file where I can make backups, quickly make as many copies as I want, and not have to worry about it getting crinkled or torn (corrupt files sometimes get uploaded or emailed, but this is a lot less common than damage to paper). When I was in school, they didn't let us use laptops so we were forced to deal with binders, paper, and textbooks and I absolutely hated it. In college my laptop almost totally replaces any paper, notebooks, textbooks, or binders.

-CDs, DVDs, blu-rays: personally, I am too young to have ever physically gone to a music store and bought a CD. Video games are going digital too now, even on consoles. I never have to touch a DVD for anything other than an OS install (this is the one thing they may remain for since I find it wears out flash drives when I reformat it a lot for OS installs, though I see flash drives which are either durable or cheap enough to be disposable happening in the near future).

Flash memory is probably better for truly long-term storage than burnable optical media or spinning rust harddrives. I've got some harddrives from the mid 90s that have siezed up from disuse because metal that sits against metal for long enough tends to stick to that metal. And in a spinning part like a harddrive, that's not good.

Optical media like CDs and DVDs rely on a dye whose state can be changed, and that dye degrades over time. faster in the light, but eventually regardless.

So, for archival purposes I'm fond of low cost flash memory.
